data.title: Zoom (ZM) vs. Twilio (TWLO): Which Communications Stock Offers More Upside?
data.description:
Zoom Communications (ZM) is reporting earnings next week, and investors will be watching for updates on the company’s growth outlook and its push beyond video conferencing. Twilio (TWLO) offers a different way to invest in communications, providing software that helps businesses engage customers through messaging, voice, and email. We compare the two stocks using the TipRanks Stock Comparison tool to see which offers more upside, according to analysts.

The comparison also shows that the two companies have market capitalizations in a similar range, making the comparison more relevant.

Is ZM a Buy Ahead of Earnings?

Zoom Communications runs the video calling and chat platform that millions of people and companies rely on for remote work, online classes, and virtual meetings. Beyond basic video calls, it sells businesses a full suite of workplace tools, including cloud phone systems, team messaging, and artificial intelligence (AI) meeting assistants. The company is set to report Q3 FY2027 earnings on November 23. According to the TipRanks forecast data, analysts estimate sales of $1.28 billion and earnings per share (EPS) of $1.49.

In its investor session last month, Zoom said it targets 6%–8% annual revenue growth by Fiscal 2030, with double-digit Enterprise growth, a non-GAAP operating margin of around 40%, and a GAAP operating margin of 28%–30%. On TipRanks, ZM has a Moderate Buy consensus, with 13 analysts rating the stock a Buy and nine rating it a Hold. The average ZM stock price target of $119.17 implies an upside of 44.62%.

Is TWLO a Buy, Sell, or Hold?

Twilio provides the behind-the-scenes software tools that companies use to build text messaging, voice calls, and email directly into their own apps. When you get a two-factor login code via text, receive an appointment reminder, or message your rideshare driver without seeing their real phone number, Twilio’s technology is usually powering it in the background. In its Q3 2026 earnings released last month, it reported revenue of $1,560 million and EPS of $1.65. For full-year 2026, it raised revenue growth from 18%–18.5% previously to 20% year-over-year.

Twilio’s top customer wins in Q3 included a health insurer that signed its first eight-figure Conversations deal to run a voice AI agent, along with AI-native firms such as ElevenLabs, Gong, and Ushur that expanded their usage. Looking ahead, TWLO has a Moderate Buy consensus from 19 Wall Street analysts, with 15 rating it a Buy, three rating it a Hold, and one rating it a Sell. The average price target of $269.39 suggests a 50.34% upside from the last price.

Conclusion

The next few quarters are important for both companies. Zoom needs to show that its expansion beyond video conferencing is gaining traction, while Twilio will be looking to build on demand for its customer-communications software. The data above offers a side-by-side view of where each company stands today. Wall Street is bullish on both stocks, but currently sees more upside in TWLO.
data.author: Sukanya Varma

data.title: SpaceX vs. Anthropic: Analysts See 90% Upside in One AI Stock
data.description:
AI companies SpaceX (SPCX) and Anthropic (ANT) are now both publicly traded. Wall Street sees very different upside potential for the two stocks. According to TipRanks’ Stock Comparison Tool, both stocks have Strong Buy consensus ratings. SpaceX’s average price target of $263.83 suggests 90% upside, while Anthropic’s average target of $133.33 points to 37% upside.

Anthropic only started trading on Nasdaq on November 19, so analyst coverage is still limited. SpaceX has wider Wall Street coverage, with 34 analysts rating the stock. It has also reported one quarter of earnings since its June IPO. SpaceX has more financial data for analysts to review, while Anthropic’s ratings may change as more analysts cover the stock.

SpaceX Delivers a Strong Q3

SpaceX reported Q3 revenue of $14.58 billion, up 161% year-over-year. Net profit reached $4.4 billion, well above the $1.8 billion forecast. AI revenue rose more than ninefold to $7.6 billion, while connectivity revenue, which includes Starlink, grew 69% to $5.25 billion.

CFO Bret Johnsen also said Q1 2027 revenue could reach $33 billion to $37 billion. That is well above the $22.2 billion analyst estimate.

Latest Analysts’ Views on SPCX

Bernstein analyst Douglas Harned kept a Buy rating on SPCX stock with a price target of $268. This points to more than 90% upside.

Harned believes the current shortage of AI computing power gives SpaceX a chance to earn back its investment fast. Elon Musk aims to add at least 20 gigawatts (GW) of power and 10GW of computing capacity by the end of 2027. SpaceX expects to have about 3GW of computing capacity by the end of 2026. The analyst expects SpaceX to charge close to $50 per watt in the first half of 2027. He said that at this price, “it can monetize the investment in less than 12 months.”

Morgan Stanley’s analyst Adam Jonas also kept his Buy rating and $300 price target on SpaceX. He called SPCX the “ultimate off-the-grid” stock because its Starlink network does not rely on the ground-based systems behind recent outages at Microsoft (MSFT) Outlook, the FAA, and the NSA. Jonas said rising demand for backup systems could help space-based internet services.

He further pointed to Starlink’s steady revenue model and plans for about $490 billion in Terafab spending through 2035. The analyst also noted that SpaceX’s 2028 earnings multiple is below that of the S&P 500.

Anthropic Q3 Revenue Soars 1,127%

Ahead of its IPO, Anthropic reported third-quarter revenue of $17 billion, up 1,127% from the same period in 2025. The company reported revenue of $33.24 billion for the nine months of 2026, up 1,200% from the same period a year ago. But Anthropic’s revenue growth slowed from one quarter to the next. Revenue rose 47% in the third quarter, down from 144% growth in the second quarter and 132% in the first quarter.

Anthropic is also still losing money. The company reported a net loss of $104 billion through September, more than four times its $25.1 billion loss in the same period last year. In the third quarter alone, its net loss reached $23.29 billion.

Wall Street’s Views on ANT Stock

Citizens’ analyst Patrick Walravens has started coverage of Anthropic (ANT) with a Buy rating and a $125 price target. He noted that Anthropic has a strong team, with all seven co-founders still at the company nearly six years after it was set up. Walravens also sees Anthropic’s approach to computing as a key strength. The company trains and runs its Claude AI model across four major chip types, giving it more ways to use computing power.

William Blair’s analyst Arjun Bhatia also started coverage of Anthropic with a Buy rating. Bhatia expects the AI market to reach at least $5 trillion. He also forecasts that Anthropic’s revenue could hit $414 billion by 2030. He values the company at 9 times its expected 2027 revenue and 6 times its 2028 revenue. Based on a 17-20 times revenue multiple, he sees Anthropic’s fair value at $130 to $150 per share.

SPCX or ANT: Which Stock Offers Higher Upside, According to Analysts?

SpaceX has an average 12-month price target of $263.83, implying 90% upside. SPCX stock has 28 Buys, six Holds, and one Sell assigned in the last three months.

ANT stock has six Buys and one Hold. In comparison, Anthropic’s average price target of $133.33 suggests 37% upside.

data.title: Marvell Stock’s (MRVL) Plunge Is My Opportunity to Buy
data.description:
Marvell Technology (MRVL) stock has taken a mighty plunge, and I see the sell-off as my opportunity to buy. At $138.47, the shares are about 56% below their record close, weighed down by broader chip-sector weakness, fears of slowing artificial intelligence (AI) spending, and dilution concerns around its pending Lumentum (LITE) acquisition. While those risks are real, I think the market has overreacted, leaving a key supplier of custom AI chips and optical data-center links trading at a steep discount just as its Lumentum deal prepares to widen its competitive moat. That risk-reward balance makes MRVL a Buy for me.

I’m selective about AI stocks right now, given how much depends on big cloud providers’ spending and how sharply that growth could slow. Still, after the recent downturn in chip stocks, I like the price I’m paying for Marvell’s growth.

When Prices Fall, I Get Excited and Buy

As a value-conscious investor, I get excited when prices fall. As Warren Buffett taught, it pays to be greedy when others are fearful.

Right now, I think we may be looking at a bottom in MRVL, with a base forming around $132 to $145 per share. The stock traded as low as $132.54 on the first Thursday in November. I managed to buy around $137, and the opportunity doesn’t look like it’s over. MRVL still trades well below its 200-day moving average, with strong forecasted fundamental growth that could carry shares to new highs before long.

What I’m Paying for Marvell’s Growth

At $138.47, I’m paying just under 20x what analysts expect Marvell to earn per share in Fiscal 2028. On November 18, the shares traded at 13.34x trailing sales, close to their five-year average of 13.55x. What excites me about that valuation is how fast earnings could grow.

Wall Street’s estimates imply about 62% annualized growth in earnings per share (EPS) from Fiscal 2028 to Fiscal 2030. Marvell’s data center revenue grew 46% year-over-year in its fiscal second quarter. While the market has sold the stock down over near-term deal dilution and AI spending concerns, I think it’s a mistake to assume strong growth won’t materialize. The recent correction gives investors a healthy margin of safety even if earnings come in somewhat below consensus.

Marvell’s Lumentum Deal Could Widen Its Moat

Part of what gives me confidence in that multi-year earnings trajectory, and helps explain why the market has been nervous, is Marvell’s pending deal for Lumentum. The deal would bring the lasers that send data through fiber-optic cables in-house. Marvell will issue new shares to pay for the deal, which the companies expect to close in the first half of 2028, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals.

Management sees more than a billion dollars in potential annual cost savings, mainly through supply-chain scale, overlapping product lines, and shared research and overhead. Even with more shares outstanding, it expects Marvell to earn more adjusted profit per share in the first year after closing than it would on its own.

The risk is that Marvell ends up with more shares splitting too little profit. Lumentum’s two largest end customers accounted for 48% of its sales in the quarter ended September 2026. If either delays orders, Lumentum’s factories still cost money to run. It would be a mistake to view this as a risk-free deal, but I think the medium-term structural upside potential far outweighs near-term sentiment concerns.

The AI Buildout Isn’t Over Yet

Perhaps most important to my MRVL thesis is that I don’t think the AI buildout is anywhere near over. I’m looking beyond the next 12 months to 2028 to judge how durable Marvell’s upside could be once spending growth slows.

Morgan Stanley (MS) expects major cloud and infrastructure companies to spend around $1.77 trillion on capital projects in 2028. That would take annual spending growth from roughly 75% in 2027 to about 7% in 2028. Some providers may even cut spending. At that pace, investors may pay less for each dollar of chipmakers’ earnings.

I think Marvell could continue to appreciate even if Nvidia (NVDA) trades sideways for a while. Moving data between chips takes power, and Marvell’s optical links can move more data per watt. That gives cloud providers a reason to keep buying even if they delay the next data center. If the facilities they’re already building fill up and generate more cash, I think spending growth could pick up again.

What Does Wall Street Think of MRVL Stock?

Wall Street rates MRVL a Strong Buy, based on 24 Buys, five Holds, and no Sells. The average 12-month analyst price target is $323.63, which implies 133.72% upside. That supports my own bullish view as a shareholder.

I’m Staying Bullish on MRVL

I’m staying bullish on MRVL after a correction I think was both healthy and due. We may see a spending cut or two, but cloud providers still have good reason to buy chips that make the data centers they’re already building cheaper to run. At this price, Marvell has the growth potential and operating quality I like. I’m holding my shares.

If the price drops below the recent low at $132.50, then I may have to watch my position more closely. However, as it stands, the medium-term fundamentals look resilient enough, and Marvell’s operations have the quality to make this a likely winning trade.

data.title: AI Investing Is Getting Riskier, but Meta and Amazon Stocks Could Come Out Ahead, Says UBS
data.description:
Wall Street is facing another turbulent period, with the scandal surrounding Nvidia adding to concerns about the outlook for AI. While the chip giant’s leadership troubles have weighed on investor sentiment, broader worries about the enormous spending required to support AI development have also contributed to market uncertainty.

Much of that concern revolves around the infrastructure needed to sustain AI growth. Data centers, advanced servers, cooling systems, and electricity supplies all require extensive investment, raising doubts about whether future revenues will justify the costs. Nevertheless, demand for computing capacity remains strong, suggesting that spending on AI infrastructure could continue growing over the coming years.

Despite these risks, UBS Chief Investment Officer Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi remains positive about the market’s prospects heading into 2027, with AI playing a central role in her outlook. In a recent note, Hoffmann-Burchardi explains why the bank expects investment to continue expanding, while warning that not every company will benefit equally.

“AI investment is accelerating, but so are the risks. We expect global AI-related investment to rise from USD 1.0 trillion in 2026 to USD 1.5 trillion in 2028, supported by constrained computing capacity and strong demand. Yet, cumulative US technology investment could approach USD 5.0 trillion by then. Revenues will probably have to reach at least USD 1.5 trillion by 2030 for the industry to earn an adequate return, and while this is possible, not every company may reap the rewards. Competition, price cuts, costly monetization, and open-weight models may threaten returns. External financing is also becoming harder, while market concentration, regulatory risks, and company-specific risks could increase volatility,” Hoffmann-Burchardi wrote.

Against this backdrop, established tech giants may be better positioned to navigate rising costs and growing competition. UBS analyst Karl Keirstead, who ranks among the top 3% of Wall Street analysts, has selected two familiar tech stocks that he believes offer solid upside potential through the end of 2027.

Adding to their appeal, both companies carry a Strong Buy consensus rating from the broader analyst community, according to the TipRanks database. Let’s take a closer look.

Meta Platforms (META)

We’ll start with Meta Platforms, the $1.58 trillion leader in the world’s social media field. The company is best known as the parent of Facebook, and its family of social media apps includes Instagram, WhatsApp, Messenger, and Threads. Together, these apps give Meta a huge reach, with the company reporting 3.64 billion daily active people across its family of apps in September 2026, up 3% from the previous year.

That reach is Meta’s greatest single advantage, as the company works to better fit its approach to today’s AI-centered world. The key to this change is the development of Muse, launched this past September. Muse is a new step in personal AI technology; rather than simply answering queries, Muse is a personal AI agent, capable of autonomously running multi-step background tasks on the user’s behalf.

Agentic AI is bursting with potential, and Meta created Muse to make use of that potential on a personal level. The AI can monitor online shopping prices or audit your subscription services to find the best deals; it can manage your emails and calendars, or even book a restaurant reservation. A small business version brings these services into the business world to manage work-related social media, or seek out new customers.

Meta’s AI forays also include the Llama family of open-source large language models, and the consumer-oriented Meta AI assistant. The company is also a leader in the VR headset field, and is developing AI-powered smart glasses. All of this takes money, however, and that brings us back to the core social media business.

Meta makes its money through selling targeted advertising space and access across its family of social apps. Meta’s ability to reach billions of people gives the company huge leverage with digital advertisers, and it shows in its earnings. In its last quarterly report, from 3Q26, Meta showed a revenue figure of $64.6 billion. This was up 26% year-over-year, and it beat the forecast by $1.2 billion. At the bottom line, Meta reported adjusted EPS of $7.40, excluding a $9.89 billion litigation charge related to a multistate legal settlement. This compared with reported GAAP earnings of $3.83 per share.

However, Meta’s heavy expenditure on expanding its AI capabilities and products comes at a price, visible in the cash flows. The cash flow from operating activities in Q3 was a solid $32.79 billion – but the free cash flow in the quarter was reported as a negative $2.12 billion.

This combination of a sound revenue foundation with high expenditures forms the core of Karl Keirstead’s thesis on Meta. In his coverage for UBS, he writes of this social media giant, “Positive investor sentiment about the prospect of Muse and Meta Business Agents may be enough to offset concerns about capex build, negative FCF and financing needs. In our view the stock at 20x 2027 GAAP EPS seems attractively priced given the recent momentum in its AI model and apps (not just infra) story. Meta is now a very different business and stock than even 18 months ago, when the company began a hard re-boot of its AI roadmap. The CEO as well as key MSL leaders are building a new ‘AI maximalist version of Meta’ and as we begin coverage of Meta shares, we will be almost singularly focused on this aspect of the story – training Muse AI models, the launch of the Muse personal agent and the push into associated business or enterprise use cases and the scaling and cost of the required compute infrastructure, benefiting from our coverage of Microsoft Azure, AWS, Google Cloud, Oracle and CoreWeave. We’ll ramp on the core Meta over time, but near-term, the AI story is driving the stock narrative.”

Keirstead is positive on the stock, in the end, and gives META shares a Buy rating and an $815 price target that implies a one-year upside potential of 32%. (To watch Keirstead’s track record, click here)

Like most of Wall Street’s tech mega-caps, Meta has picked up a lot of analyst reviews, 43 on file right now. These split into 37 Buys and 6 Holds, giving the stock its Strong Buy consensus rating. META is currently priced at $616.38, and its average price target of $857.24 suggests that it will gain 39% by this time next year. (See META stock forecast)

Amazon (AMZN)

The UBS pick we’ll look at is Amazon, another of Wall Street’s trillion-dollar-plus giants. Amazon is a dot-com survivor, and has built itself up into the world’s largest online retailer, and in fact, its only true peer in the ‘retail giant’ space is Walmart.

But where Walmart is primarily a retailer, Amazon has expanded into several other industries, with its North America and International segments accounting for about 82% of total revenue in 2025. While its online retail segment will never go away, and will provide a large-scale revenue stream, Amazon is working steadily to increase its non-retail footprint – and AI is central to that plan.

At the center of Amazon’s non-retail expansion is AWS, the company’s cloud computing platform, which provides infrastructure, storage, AI tools, and other services to customers worldwide. AWS is among the fastest-growing of Amazon’s various businesses, and has shown rapid expansion in recent years – the Q3 report showed that AWS generated $46 billion in revenue, for a 39% year-over-year gain, far higher than the 5% to 6% growth recorded by Amazon’s International and North America segments. AWS is known for its wide-ranging set of cloud-based tools and apps, and in recent years Amazon has been adding AI to that mix.

Amazon is also involved in the ‘back end’ of AI. The company has entered the AI-capable silicon chip business, with its Trainium semiconductor. This is an in-house custom-built AI accelerator family, and it has attracted attention from some of the AI model providers. Anthropic, the company behind Claude, has committed to using up to 5 gigawatts of AWS Trainium capacity, while OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, has agreed to consume about 2 gigawatts, with deployment beginning to ramp up in 2027.

When we zoom out a bit, and look at Amazon’s overall 3Q26 report, we see that the company’s AI exposure is clearly leading its growth. Amazon’s net revenue in Q3 was up 12% from 3Q25, and hit $201.9 billion; we should note that this figure was nearly $340 million below expectations. Of the total revenue, AWS’s $46 billion made up approximately 23%. Amazon’s EPS in the third quarter of $1.89 was down 6 cents per share from the year-ago period’s $1.95 figure. Amazon attributed the year-over-year earnings decrease primarily to $9.5 billion in pre-tax gains from its Anthropic investments recorded during the third quarter of 2025.

Once again, UBS is bullish on a major-name tech giant. Keirstead says of Amazon, “AI model and chip agnostic nature of AWS will help position Amazon shares as a defensive AI play and an AI enabler to enterprises scaling their AI investments in 2027+. These positives outweigh the impact on AWS growth from quarterly variability in the model API access revenue stream. In terms of our AWS estimates, we’re trimming our revs growth estimates (for 4Q26 to 41% from 42%, for 2027 to 43% from 48%) and our margin estimate (for 2027 to 40% from 45%). Amazon is now a very different business than even 2-3 years ago and the investment research process needs to change with it, to break from the past. The AWS cloud segment, while still only 23% of revs, represented 60% of Amazon’s y/y revs growth in 3Q26, 63% of EBIT dollars, likely 70%+ of capex, and Amazon’s AI/AWS narrative and outlook dominate the investor debate.”

Quantifying his stance on Amazon, the top-rated tech expert sets a Buy rating with a $340 price target that indicates his confidence in a 27% gain for the next 12 months.

Wall Street is also bullish on Amazon, and the stock has a solid Strong Buy consensus rating, based on 43 recent reviews with a decidedly lopsided split of 42 Buys to just 1 Hold. The stock’s trading price of $267.74 and average target price of $324.41 together suggest an upside of 21% on the one-year horizon. (See AMZN stock forecast)

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed in this article are solely those of the featured analysts. The content is intended to be used for informational purposes only. It is very important to do your own analysis before making any investment.

data.title: Palo Alto Networks Stock Jumps as AI Cyber Threats Create New Growth Opportunity
data.description:
Shares of cybersecurity company Palo Alto Networks (PANW) jumped on Thursday after the company lifted its annual outlook. Meanwhile, CEO Nikesh Arora warned that serious software vulnerabilities are being discovered at nearly seven times last year’s monthly average. This could benefit Palo Alto by increasing demand for its virtual patching and AI security services, which would help the company generate additional recurring revenue.

Arora explained on Wednesday that security teams are struggling to install software fixes fast enough. Meanwhile, a recent AI-assisted hacking campaign targeted at least 19 organizations, with attackers gaining unauthorized access to systems or data at 10 of them.

Researchers from Palo Alto’s Unit 42 division uncovered the operation, which took place during August and September. The attackers used an open-source AI tool called Cairn to carry out 25 operations. At one organization, more than one million personal records were exposed. The software could plan attacks and adjust its approach without requiring someone to oversee every step.

This creates another problem for businesses. Even when software developers release security updates, companies cannot always install them immediately without the risk of disruptions to their systems. Arora expects that the heavy workload associated with these updates could continue for at least another 18 months.

Catalysts That May Push the Stock Higher

The growing number of software vulnerabilities could increase demand for Palo Alto’s virtual patching service, which protects vulnerable systems while companies prepare permanent fixes. Palo Alto already serves nearly 70,000 network security customers, giving it a sizable existing customer base for the service.

Meanwhile, demand for AI security is already contributing to the company’s growth. Its Prisma AIRS product reached nearly $170 million in annual recurring revenue within five quarters of becoming available, with more than 1,000 customers using the platform. Furthermore, traffic generated by AI agents on Palo Alto’s network security platform increased about ninefold year-over-year.

Yesterday’s earnings provided additional evidence of strong cybersecurity spending. Fiscal first-quarter revenue grew by 39% to $3.44 billion, while next-generation security annual recurring revenue increased by 66% to $9.73 billion.

Risks to Watch Out For

However, the sevenfold increase refers to discovered software vulnerabilities, not successful cyberattacks. AI can also help security teams find weaknesses before hackers exploit them. Therefore, the longer-term effect on cybersecurity spending remains uncertain.

Additionally, Palo Alto faces competition from other security providers, and some customers may prefer upgrading their existing tools rather than purchasing additional services.

The company’s valuation is another consideration. Palo Alto trades at roughly 82 times the midpoint of its projected Fiscal 2027 adjusted earnings of $4.26 to $4.30 per share. This leaves less room for disappointing results if demand for its newer AI security products slows down.

Is PANW Stock a Good Buy?

Turning to Wall Street, TipRanks data shows that analysts have a Strong Buy consensus rating on PANW stock. This is based on 32 Buys and eight Holds assigned in the past three months. Furthermore, the average PANW price target of $423.43 per share implies 17.1% upside potential. (See PANW Stock Forecast).

data.title: 3 ‘Strong Buy’ Data Center Stocks to Watch After Anthropic’s Record IPO
data.description:
AI developer Anthropic (ANT) began trading on Thursday on Nasdaq. It raised a record $81.34 billion in its initial public offering (IPO), above its earlier target due to strong demand. This has drawn fresh attention to the AI trade. For investors looking for other ways to gain exposure to the industry, analysts remain bullish on three less popular data center-related names: Willdan Group (WLDN), Comfort Systems (FIX), and Graham Corporation (GHM). Each stock carries a Strong Buy rating from analysts with at least 50% upside, according to TipRanks’ Compare Top Data Center Stocks tool.

GHM has rallied the most year-to-date, up 23% to about $77 per share. However, Willdan offers the biggest upside of 78%.

These companies are among the “pick and shovels” of the AI buildout. They provide the physical infrastructure that powers the data center boom.

Willdan Group (WLDN)

Willdan is an American engineering and construction company. It helps companies maximize their energy systems and modernize their electric grids. It also offers consulting on building and safety guidance.

The company’s clients span utilities, government agencies, and private businesses.

Concerns surrounding its leadership transition, extensive spending commitments, and the sustainability of AI infrastructure investments continue weighing on sentiment.

And if investor Sungarden Investment is correct, the worst may still lie ahead. Despite Nvidia’s already steep losses, the investor believes the stock could tumble all the way to $100 over the next 12 to 18 months. His warning rests primarily on technical indicators and broader market conditions, suggesting that Nvidia’s troubles extend well beyond the controversy surrounding former CEO Jensen Huang.

Sungarden’s bearish outlook begins with a comparison between current trading patterns and previous market downturns. Although Nvidia has recovered from several steep sell-offs over the past decade, the investor believes this episode could prove far more damaging.

“While I always account for the possibility that any stock or ETF can manage yet another big leg up, I think the odds are against NVDA this time,” Sungarden noted.

Sungarden believes institutional selling could continue overwhelming buying interest, preventing a lasting recovery despite Nvidia’s technological advantages. The investor also points to deteriorating liquidity, suggesting that large investment funds may be reducing their exposure to leading tech companies.

Another concern involves the financial relationships supporting the industry’s rapid expansion, where investments move between cloud providers, developers, and semiconductor manufacturers. Sungarden points out that these arrangements could become problematic for Nvidia if financing slows, while Huang’s departure introduces additional uncertainty surrounding strategic direction.

However, the investor considers broader trading mechanics more important than any individual controversy, especially when examining heavily weighted equities like Nvidia during prolonged market downturns.

“In a liquidity-driven unwind, the generals are always the last to get taken out. And their drop is the steepest,” Sungarden explained.

Essentially, Sungarden argues that Nvidia’s dominant position within passive portfolios could become a liability when investors withdraw capital from index funds. Those withdrawals could increase selling pressure on heavily weighted stocks like Nvidia, potentially creating additional downward momentum regardless of underlying financial performance.

His Nvidia chart analysis also reveals deteriorating momentum, with several important moving averages already broken and successive rallies failing to establish stronger price levels.

Ultimately, Sungarden offers a particularly bearish forecast for investors expecting Nvidia to recover its previous valuation: “To $100, more likely than back to $240, its previous peak level, over the next 12-18 months.” (To watch Sungarden Investment’s track record, click here)

data.title: ‘A Blessing in Disguise,’ Says Investor About Micron Stock
data.description:
Nvidia’s leadership crisis has kept investors on edge for the past couple of weeks. It began when reports surfaced that Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman U.S. officials suspect of spying for China. He resigned as CEO on Nov. 12, and chip stocks were hit hard on Monday when worries about his exit came on top of new U.S. export rules. A better-than-expected quarter on Tuesday didn’t stop Nvidia’s slide either.

Micron (NASDAQ:MU) has been one of the AI stocks affected by the fallout. And despite the shares gaining today as Anthropic goes public, the stock still sits roughly 38% below its June peak.

While the market evidently did not like Huang’s resignation and the board’s refusal to consider his return, investor Chetan Woodun thinks the Huang affair could turn out to help the American AI trade, and Micron with it.

The argument starts in Washington. If investigators find that Beijing was trying to get at sensitive chip technology, the affair becomes a national security case. That could bring Republicans and Democrats together behind domestic chipmaking and AI infrastructure, and behind tighter limits on what reaches China. A first step has already happened. On Nov. 16, the Commerce Department said exporters now need a license to send advanced AI chips to overseas data centers that rent computing power to Chinese firms. Huang had long argued for selling to China, so the investor thinks his exit could make tougher rules easier to pass.

That matters for Micron because its high-bandwidth memory (HBM) goes inside the same AI accelerators Washington wants to keep away from China. Woodun also likes that Micron doesn’t depend on a single buyer. Its HBM3E chips are used in AMD’s Instinct MI350 line, and the investor thinks AMD could gain ground if Nvidia struggles under new leadership. Micron’s latest annual report shows that no customer made up 10% of sales in fiscal 2026. A year earlier, one customer accounted for 17%.

Demand looks solid. Speaking at the TomorrowX Summit in Austin on Wednesday, CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said 75% of Micron’s 2027 output is already sold and that talks have moved on to 2028. He expects memory supply in 2027 and 2028 to be even tighter than this year. Even so, the stock trades below 5x forward earnings, and Woodun thinks Micron has earned a higher multiple.

The investor does see risks. Memory has a long record of booms followed by painful busts. The Fed raised rates in September and is expected to raise them again in December, which hurts debt-funded customers like CoreWeave. Data centers are also drawing criticism for the strain they put on power grids and water supplies. China worries Woodun less. Memory isn’t the main target of U.S. export rules, and Micron expects China to make up a single-digit share of revenue in fiscal 2027.

In the end, Woodun’s view is that one company’s leadership crisis doesn’t derail the AI spending cycle, and that it may even strengthen it by keeping China further behind.

Accordingly, Woodun rates MU stock a Buy. (To watch Woodun’s track record, click here)

So do most Street analysts. Based on 28 Buys vs. 1 Hold, consensus views this stock as a Strong Buy. Going by the $1,624 average price target, a year from now, shares will be changing hands for a 118% premium. (See Micron stock forecast)

data.title: Someone’s Betting Against AMD Stock, and This Investor Sees a Better AI Bet Elsewhere
data.description:
When Nvidia lost its founder and CEO last week, the money leaving its shares stayed in the AI chip trade. Much of it went to Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) and Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO), the two names usually pitched as the alternatives. A week on, one of them has a problem of its own.

AMD fell as much as 11% on Thursday after short seller Hunterbrook disclosed a bet against the stock. Hunterbrook alleges that a blacklisted Chinese server maker kept receiving updated AMD firmware, and it questions how much AMD finances the customers buying its chips. AMD pushed back, telling Bloomberg that Hunterbrook’s claims “misrepresent” its business practices and relationships and that it follows US export control rules.

The latest news makes a useful backdrop for a recent analysis by an investor using the moniker of Millennial Dividends (MD), who, before the short report was released, wondered which of the two is better placed to benefit from Nvidia’s troubles. MD is less focused on the leadership change than on Nvidia’s roadmap. Kyber, the rack meant for 2027’s Rubin Ultra chips, has reportedly slipped to 2028 because of a hard-to-make circuit board. Rubin Ultra itself has reportedly been cut from four compute dies to two. MD thinks the CEO exit could drag those delays out.

AMD is doing fine on its own, with third-quarter revenue up 45% year over year to $13.4 billion and guidance for more than 80% growth in 2027. If hyperscalers need capacity in 2027 that Nvidia can’t deliver, MD sees them buying more MI450 chips as “capacity insurance,” even though moving code off Nvidia’s CUDA software is costly. Still, AMD is unlikely to become the main supplier, and more competition could squeeze chip prices. Whether that actually lifts AMD’s revenue growth is, in MD’s view, anyone’s guess.

Broadcom’s setup is cleaner. Fiscal third-quarter AI chip revenue more than tripled YoY to $16.7 billion, and CEO Hock Tan is targeting about $115 billion in AI revenue for fiscal 2027. Broadcom co-designs the custom chips, or XPUs, that hyperscalers buy instead of Nvidia GPUs, under deals with Google through 2031 and Meta through 2029. Its Tomahawk Ethernet switches go into Nvidia clusters and custom ones alike, so a delayed Nvidia rack makes little difference to it. The risks are a gross margin guided down to about 73% from 78% a year earlier, as XPUs take a bigger share of sales, and a concentrated customer base.

Valuation widens the gap. Broadcom trades at about 18x its fiscal 2027 consensus EPS of $19.47. Even after Thursday’s drop, AMD sits near 27x its 2027 estimate of $17.69. MD sees little room for error in AMD’s price. AMD could still come out ahead if it takes real share from Nvidia, but Broadcom gets paid whichever way Nvidia’s roadmap goes. That’s why MD is holding off on buying any more AMD shares right now and keeps Broadcom as the top pick. (To watch Millennial Dividends’ track record, click here)

On the Street, both these stocks are considered Strong Buys. Over the next year, AMD is expected to gain 34%, given the average target clocks in at $652.18. AVGO’s average target lands at $514.86, implying the shares will climb by 45% over the 12-month timeframe. (See AMD stock forecast or AVGO stock forecast)

data.title: ‘The Market Already Knows,’ Says Investor About Nvidia Stock
data.description:
Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) has spent the past year showing that strong quarters and a rising share price don’t always go together. Its third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday followed the same pattern. Results beat expectations and the outlook came in stronger, yet the shares gave up an early jump on Wednesday and closed lower. This time there was an extra weight on the stock. It was the first report since Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Nov. 12, and the question of who runs Nvidia next is still unresolved.

The board says Huang won’t be back, and Bloomberg reports it is now courting Arm CEO Rene Haas. The stock now sits more than a third below its October record.

That gap between the business and the stock is where investor Vladimir Dimitrov puts his focus. He has no quarrel with the latest results, but he thinks the share price already reflects near-term expectations, so the useful signals sit in what the guidance implies.

Growth is a good example. Revenue more than doubled year over year for a second straight quarter, and management raised its early fiscal 2028 forecast to about 75% growth, from 70%. Dimitrov doesn’t think that changes much. He believes the market is bracing for several years of slowing growth, which is why Nvidia’s price-to-sales multiple has kept shrinking through a run of beats. The shares now trade at less than 11 times forward earnings. He sees the second quarter as the likely peak. YoY growth slipped from 106% then to 103% in the third quarter, and the guide implies about 90% for the fourth.

Margins follow a similar path. Gross margin topped guidance last quarter, but Nvidia expects it to bottom at 71%–72% this quarter before settling at 72%–73% in fiscal 2028, while operating expenses climb to nearly $11 billion. Further out, memory costs could ease and lift margins back toward 75%, but Dimitrov sees pricing power and hyperscaler demand as risks.

That last one worries him most. By his numbers, combined capex at Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Oracle jumped 118% YoY in the third quarter and now exceeds operating cash flow for four of the five. He sees a real chance that 2026 marks the top for spending by some of Nvidia’s biggest customers. He also flagged interim CEO Colette Kress saying on the call that the company is “rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments and guarantees,” which he reads as a sign the easy gains are behind it.

Dimitrov’s base case is that growth, margins and hyperscaler demand all peak in 2026. In his view, the stock can keep posting great numbers and still do no better than the broader market.

As such, he rates NVDA a Hold (i.e., Neutral). (To watch Dimitrov’s track record, click here)

data.title: Fortinet (FTNT) vs. Zscaler (ZS): Which Cybersecurity Stock Offers More Upside?
data.description:
Fortinet (FTNT) and Zscaler (ZS) stand to gain as Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin warns of rising cyber threats to U.S. critical infrastructure, though Wall Street sees higher upside in one. The warning indicated that criminals are using advanced artificial intelligence (AI) to carry out more cyberattacks and identify potential targets. The comments come as U.S. officials also highlighted threats to transportation, healthcare, water, and energy systems.

These cybersecurity stocks take different approaches, with Fortinet providing network security and firewall solutions, while Zscaler focuses on securing cloud access, applications, and data. We compared the two stocks using the TipRanks Stock Comparison tool to see which offers more upside, according to analysts. The tool can also help to compare stocks based on market cap, P/E ratio, Smart Score, dividend yield, and more.

Is FTNT Stock a Buy?

Fortinet is a U.S.-based cybersecurity company that provides network security and firewall solutions for businesses and government organizations. Its Security Fabric platform is designed to protect networks, endpoints, applications, and cloud environments. It has recently pushed into AI security, launching the FortiGuard Inline AI Security Service, which adds AI-specific inspection and guardrails for FortiGate customers through a cloud-delivered service. Founder, Chairman, and CEO Ken Xie said Q3 reflected strong execution and broad-based demand across the entire portfolio, which let the company raise its 2026 billings guidance for the third time this year.

In Q3 2026, revenue grew 20% year-over-year to $2.08 billion, product revenue rose 37% to $765 million, and billings grew 29% to $2.34 billion. Earnings per share (EPS) climbed 23% to $0.91. For full-year 2026, Fortinet now expects revenue of $8.125 billion to $8.215 billion and billings of $9.568 billion to $9.718 billion, with EPS of $3.54 to $3.58. The board also authorized an additional $1.2 billion in share repurchases.

On TipRanks, Fortinet has a ‘Perfect 10’ Smart Score. The average stock price target of $150.76 implies a 10.07% upside. 18 analysts rate the stock a Hold, seven rate it a Buy, and four analysts rate it a Sell. Overall, FTNT has a Hold consensus rating.

Is Zscaler a Buy, Sell, or Hold?

Zscaler provides cloud-based zero-trust security through its Zero Trust Exchange platform. The platform helps organizations control access to applications and data based on user identity, device security, and business policies, rather than relying on traditional network-based defenses. CEO Jay Chaudhry said the agentic AI era is quickly becoming the most significant opportunity in the company’s history and that Zscaler is working toward a $10 billion ARR target.

In Q4 2026, revenue was $898.2 million, up 25% year-over-year, and adjusted EPS was $1.19 against estimates of $1.09. Full-year FY26 revenue rose 25% to $3.353 billion. Zscaler also expects $30 million to $33 million in restructuring charges, mostly in the first half of FY27. Also, growth in customers with ARR above $1 million has slowed over recent quarters.

Zscaler has a TipRanks Smart Score of 7. It has a Strong Buy consensus, with 30 of the 36 analysts covering the stock rating the stock a Buy. The average ZS stock price target of $239.50 suggests a 12.22% upside from recent price levels.

Conclusion

The growing use of AI is changing both the nature of cyberattacks and the tools companies need to defend against them. Fortinet is building on its network-security and firewall expertise, while Zscaler is positioning its cloud-based Zero Trust platform for a world where users, devices, and applications operate beyond traditional network boundaries. The data above offers a side-by-side view of where each company stands today. Wall Street currently sees more upside in ZS.

data.title: ‘Follow the Cash,’ Says Top Investor About Oracle Stock
data.description:
On the day Wall Street finally gets its hands on a frontier AI lab, Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) shareholders have reason to look past the party. Anthropic starts trading on the Nasdaq today after pricing above its marketed range in the largest IPO ever. OpenAI, the lab that matters most to Oracle, is still private and is reportedly aiming for a 2027 listing.

That matters because Oracle’s growth plans depend heavily on OpenAI being able to keep raising money. OpenAI accounts for nearly half of Oracle’s backlog, and the ChatGPT maker’s latest private round has reportedly reached $15 billion, half of its original goal. Anthropic just showed that public investors will hand an AI lab $81.3 billion in one go, but OpenAI can’t tap that pool yet.

Oracle shares currently trade almost two-thirds below their September 2025 record.

Keith Noonan, who contributes to The Motley Fool and ranks among the top 3% of investors on TipRanks, sees that reliance on a single customer as a big reason Wall Street has lost its nerve on the stock.

Oracle closed its fiscal first quarter on Aug. 31 with $664 billion in remaining performance obligations, meaning work customers have signed up for that hasn’t turned into revenue yet. At least $300 billion of that is widely thought to come from OpenAI. The investor points out that the contract terms aren’t public. Oracle would probably collect cancellation fees if OpenAI pulled back, but a fee is only worth something if the customer can pay it. In his view, Oracle has staked its future on OpenAI growing into its commitments. Noonan adds that this kind of exposure bites harder in AI infrastructure, where data centers cost a fortune to build and run.

So far, the results show no strain. First-quarter revenue rose 30% year over year to $19.3 billion, cloud sales jumped 62% to $11.6 billion, and adjusted EPS climbed 30% to $1.92. At today’s price, the stock trades at roughly 14 times the $8.10 in non-GAAP EPS management is guiding to for fiscal 2027. Noonan agrees those numbers make Oracle look cheap, but he doesn’t think they tell the full story.

The cash flow statement is less comfortable. Oracle brought in $23 billion in operating cash during the quarter but spent about $28.5 billion on capex, leaving free cash flow at negative $5 billion. Because a data center counts as an investment on the balance sheet rather than a cost on the income statement, the investor notes, reported earnings understate how much money is going out the door. Oracle is plugging the gap with borrowing and share sales. It carries about $125 billion in debt, plans $90 billion to $95 billion in capex this fiscal year, and will probably keep spending big after that.

For Noonan, fast growth and a low multiple don’t outweigh a debt-funded build-out tied this closely to one customer, and he sees Oracle stock as riskier than its earnings make it look. (To watch Noonan’s track record, click here)

Most on the Street, however, take an optimistic stance here. Based on a mix of 28 Buys, 4 Holds and 1 Sell, the analyst consensus rates the stock a Strong Buy. At $241.83, the average price target implies shares will gain 111% in the months ahead. (See ORCL stock forecast)

data.title: DELL, MRVL, ADI: 3 AI Stocks to Buy Ahead of Next Week’s Earnings, According to Analysts
data.description:
AI hardware and chip stocks Dell Technologies (DELL), Analog Devices (ADI), and Marvell Technology (MRVL) will report their quarterly results next week. Analog Devices and Dell are both slated to report on Tuesday, November 24, followed by Marvell on Thursday, November 26.

The three companies serve different parts of the tech sector. Dell makes AI servers, Analog Devices supplies chips, and Marvell makes custom chips for data centers. According to TipRanks data, analysts see the most upside in Marvell at 122.36%. Dell follows at 88.21%, while Analog Devices offers 26.55%.

Here is the breakdown of all three stocks and what Wall Street expects from them.

Dell Technologies (NYSE:DELL)

Dell Technologies provides IT systems for businesses, including AI servers, storage, and PCs. Demand for AI servers has helped build its backlog to $95 billion.

Dell is scheduled to report its fiscal Q3 2027 results after the market closes on November 24. Wall Street expects adjusted earnings of $6.60 per share, up sharply from $2.59 in the year-ago quarter. Revenue is projected to jump roughly 82% year-over-year to $49.25 billion.

According to TipRanks, DELL stock has a Moderate Buy consensus rating based on 14 Buys and seven Holds assigned over the past three months. At $589.32, the average analyst price target implies 88.21% upside from current levels.

Analog Devices (NASDAQ:ADI)

Analog Devices makes chips that process real-world signals. Its products are used in factories, cars, communications systems, and data centers.

The company will report its fiscal Q4 2026 results before the market opens on November 24. Analysts expect Analog Devices to post earnings of $3.89 per share, up from $2.26 a year earlier. Meanwhile, quarterly revenue is projected to reach $4.32 billion.

On TipRanks, ADI carries a Strong Buy consensus rating based on 16 Buys and one Hold. Its average 12-month price target of $483.40 implies 26.55% upside potential.

Marvell Technology (NASDAQ:MRVL)

Marvell Technology makes chips that help data centers handle AI workloads. Its products support AI computing and high-speed data links.

Marvell is estimated to announce its fiscal Q3 2027 results on November 26. Wall Street forecasts MRVL to report adjusted earnings of $1.10 per share, representing a 44.7% increase from $0.76 per share in the same period last year. Revenue is expected to surge 52.2% year-over-year to $3.15 billion.

 Marvell currently holds a Strong Buy consensus rating on TipRanks, based on 24 Buys and five Holds issued in the last three months. Marvell’s average analyst price target of $323.63 points to 122.36% upside from current levels.

data.title: ‘Don’t Be a Fool,’ Says Investor About Anthropic Stock
data.description:
What a difference one blockbuster IPO can make to Wall Street’s mood after several turbulent weeks. With Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT) arriving on Thursday, investors seem willing to overlook recent tech losses, the controversy surrounding Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang, fears about excessive AI expenditures, and uncertainty stemming from the Democrats’ midterm victories.

The excitement surrounding the Claude developer is understandable, considering its $83 offering price, record $81.3 billion IPO, and valuation of about $1.5 trillion. With the broader market surging, investors appear ready to embrace what could become one of the most closely watched listings in history.

Yet, investor Rafa Oliver believes the enthusiasm surrounding Anthropic may be getting ahead of financial reality. Despite recognizing the company’s technological achievements and rapid expansion, Oliver sees serious risks for anyone purchasing shares at current valuations.

Oliver makes his central concern clear in his analysis, writing, “My doubt is the price, and it comes from how I see the business: Anthropic sells work that gets cheaper with every new model, it has two rivals with deep pockets, and to keep up with them, it has to rent its computers years before it knows how much it will sell.”

Anthropic has already committed about $900.9 billion toward computing infrastructure, creating considerable financial obligations should customer demand fall short of expectations.

Meanwhile, competition from OpenAI and Google could limit pricing flexibility, making sustained profitability harder to achieve. Oliver estimates that annual revenue could reach $766.6 billion by 2036, giving the Claude creator a commanding 68% share of his projected industry opportunity.

However, even those assumptions fail to support the original $74 IPO midpoint, let alone the final $83 offering price. According to his calculations, operating margins would need to improve far beyond historical levels to justify even the earlier valuation.

Computing costs represent another concern, having consumed 48.1% of sales during Anthropic’s strongest reported quarter. Oliver estimates that this figure would need to fall to 26.2% for the earlier pricing assumptions to make financial sense.

Employee compensation introduces further complications, with stock-based awards potentially reducing intrinsic value by $31.29 per share. Such dilution could erode returns for long-term holders, regardless of how successfully Anthropic expands its operations.

Oliver also believes investors should consider how much future growth is already reflected in today’s valuation. His model assigns the company a fair value of just $46.26 per share, which would represent about 44% downside from the final $83 IPO price.

And when it comes to deciding whether investors should participate in the highly anticipated debut, Oliver leaves little room for interpretation: “On listing day, I would not buy.” His conclusion reflects his belief that Anthropic’s valuation already exceeds what its financial prospects can justify.
